analysis.one_liner: Ends a tax deduction that lets the largest oil companies reduce their taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill to strip the biggest oil companies of a multibillion-dollar tax deduction died in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would deny large oil companies — those producing at least 500,000 barrels of crude per day — the "domestic production" tax deduction they can claim on income from making, refining, and moving oil and gas [S2]. That deduction is worth billions a year to the handful of biggest oil companies; ending it would have raised federal revenue from them [S3]. It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never went anywhere [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, in two ways: the government would collect more tax revenue from major oil companies, revenue that could reduce deficits or offset other taxes, and the largest oil companies would no longer receive a special break smaller energy companies cannot claim [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the tax code so that a "major integrated oil company" — one with average daily worldwide production of at least 500,000 barrels of crude oil and gross receipts over $1 billion — can no longer claim the section 199 deduction for income from producing, refining, processing, transporting, or distributing oil and gas [S2][S3].
The change applies to taxable years beginning after enactment, so the deduction would end going forward rather than retroactively [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The largest integrated oil companies — the handful of firms big enough to meet the production and revenue thresholds — would pay billions more in taxes, and the industry warned that costs could be passed through to consumers [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Oil companies argued that stripping the deduction would raise their operating costs and that some of that cost would show up at the pump, since domestic oil and gas production decisions are sensitive to tax treatment [S2].

The section 199 deduction applies to many kinds of manufacturers; singling out oil and gas companies is a targeted penalty on one industry that supporters of the deduction said put domestic energy production at a disadvantage relative to foreign producers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is simple: the bill would have taken billions in annual tax savings away from the largest oil companies and left that money with the federal government, at the risk of modestly higher fuel costs or less domestic drilling investment. The revenue was the point — but the bill never got far enough for anyone to weigh that trade-off in public.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which controls tax bills, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 3, 2011 by Rep. Timothy Bishop with 50 original cosponsors, all Democrats [S3].
On the day of introduction it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation [S5].
Fifty-six members cosponsored the bill, all of them Democrats [S4].

No further action was ever taken on the bill; it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in the House or Senate, and it died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The major oil companies kept their annual tax deduction, and the members of Congress with authority over tax bills were spared a vote on repealing it. Taxpayers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Major oil companies and Ways and Means leaders

for.name: Rep. Timothy Bishop
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to deny the oil and gas deduction to major integrated oil companies.

for.name: 56 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a hearing or vote on it before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party in the 112th House, which set the Ways and Means agenda and the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Bills repealing oil and gas tax breaks were not brought to a vote as free-standing measures; oil industry tax provisions moved only when paired with things the industry favored.

sides.party_line_note: All 56 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; the House majority was Republican, and the bill never advanced past referral in the Republican-controlled Ways and Means Committee [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would strip firms producing at least 500,000 barrels of crude per day of the domestic production tax deduction on their oil and gas income, a break worth billions annually to the largest companies [S2][S3]. Keeping it preserved their tax advantage; the bill died.

industries.industry: Smaller domestic oil and gas producers
industries.note: The bill targeted only the largest companies, so smaller producers' relative tax position would have improved without any change to their own taxes [S2].
